cards.a: They are what makes SPA navigations start to look like native app transitions — a crossfade or a shared element morphing from list to detail — with no animation library and no manual FLIP maths.

cards.t: Node 16 · Blocking navigation and the platform
cards.q: What is the general pattern this node illustrates?
cards.a: The platform slowly absorbing what libraries simulated. Routers built click interception, history reasoning and transition animation by hand for fifteen years; the browser is now shipping first-class versions of each.

cards.t: Node 16 · Blocking navigation and the platform
cards.q: A user closes the tab with an unsaved draft and loses it. What should you have done, and what is the better answer?
cards.a: A beforeunload listener registered only while the draft is dirty. The better answer is autosaving the draft so the question does not arise — prompts are a fallback, not a design.

cards.t: Node 16 · Blocking navigation and the platform
cards.q: Why is the Navigation API significant even though it is Chromium-only?
cards.a: Because it collapses click interception, form interception, back/forward handling, scroll and focus into one event with a real preventDefault — replacing most of the fragile machinery routers hand-built for fifteen years.

cards.t: Node 16 · Blocking navigation and the platform
cards.q: What does event.intercept({ handler }) do that preventDefault alone cannot?
cards.a: It tells the browser you are handling this navigation asynchronously, so the browser keeps the URL, tracks it as an ongoing navigation, and applies its own scroll and focus behaviour when your handler resolves.

cards.q: What are the three axes routers differ along?
cards.a: How routes are declared (config object, components, or filesystem), whether the router owns data (pure matcher versus loaders and actions), and whether it is type-safe (are bad paths a compile error, are params typed).

cards.q: What is file-based routing and what does it eliminate?
cards.a: Directory structure is the route tree — app/routes/products/[id].tsx. It removes the "I forgot to register the route" class of bug and makes the route table discoverable by tooling, which is why Next.js, Remix, SvelteKit and Nuxt all use it.

cards.q: What is the cost of file-based routing?
cards.a: Route structure is coupled to file layout, dynamic or runtime-computed routes are awkward, and each framework invents its own filename conventions — brackets, dollars, parentheses, underscores — which are not transferable.

cards.q: Summarise React Router's version history.
cards.a: v3 and earlier: static config. v4 (March 2017): everything is a component, dynamic routing. v6 (2021): ranking, nesting, <Outlet>, useNavigate. v6.4 (September 2022): route objects with loaders and actions. v7 (late 2024): merged with Remix so one library covers a plain SPA and a full-stack framework.

cards.q: Why does knowing that history matter practically?
cards.a: Because the versions are genuinely different products. Answers, code samples and tutorials from the v4 era are wrong for v6 — exact, <Switch>, render props and useHistory are all gone.

cards.q: What is TanStack Router's pitch?
cards.a: End-to-end type safety — a mistyped path is a compile error, params and search params are typed, and search params are validated by a schema per route — plus loaders and an integrated cache. Version 1.0 arrived in late 2023.

cards.q: When does TanStack Router's cost pay off?
cards.a: When the URL carries a lot of structured state — dashboards, data tables, filter-heavy tools — where typed, validated search params replace a pile of hand-written parsing.

cards.q: What is wouter?
cards.a: A roughly 2 kB minimal matcher with a hooks API. The right answer when you need three screens and nothing else, or when bundle size dominates.

cards.q: How does Vue Router differ in shape?
cards.a: Config-based route arrays, <router-view> as the outlet, and navigation guards as a first-class API — beforeEach globally, beforeEnter per route, and in-component guards. Guards are more central than in React Router.

cards.q: What does Angular's router already have that React arrived at later?
cards.a: Resolvers — per-route data loading before activation, which are loaders under another name and predate them by years — plus CanActivate and CanDeactivate guard interfaces. The convergence is real and worth saying out loud.

cards.q: What does the convergence across frameworks tell you?
cards.a: That the problems are inherent to routing, not to any framework: match, nest, load data before render, guard, contain errors, handle pending states, and manage focus. Every ecosystem reinvents them in a different order.

cards.q: Give a practical router-selection heuristic.
cards.a: Needs SEO or a server: reach for a meta-framework rather than bolting SSR onto a SPA. Behind a login, client-rendered: React Router in data mode. URL carrying lots of structured state: TanStack Router. Three screens: wouter, or the twenty lines from Nodes 3 and 4.

cards.q: Why is "write your own router" a legitimate answer sometimes?
cards.a: Because Nodes 3 and 4 are twenty lines. For a small internal tool with a handful of static screens, a library is more configuration than the problem deserves — and knowing you could is what makes the choice informed rather than default.

cards.q: What is the one thing every router shares, no matter the API?
cards.a: They all wrap pushState, replaceState and popstate, and they all intercept anchor clicks. Everything above that is ergonomics, matching strategy, and how much of Nodes 9 through 15 they hand you.

cards.q: A tutorial uses <Switch>, useHistory and exact. What version is it, and what are the equivalents now?
cards.a: React Router v5. <Switch> became <Routes>, useHistory became useNavigate, and exact is gone because matching is exact by default.

cards.q: Your app is a client-rendered internal dashboard behind a login with heavy filtering. Which router and why?
cards.a: React Router in data mode is the safe default; TanStack Router earns its cost here specifically because the URL carries a lot of structured filter state that benefits from typed, schema-validated search params.

cards.q: Someone proposes adding SSR to an existing client-only SPA for SEO. What is the honest advice?
cards.a: Retrofitting SSR usually means adopting a meta-framework, because you need routing both server and client understand plus hydration. If SEO is the driver, evaluate that migration rather than bolting a render server onto the existing app.
